prose_changes.old: Grew out of the Jesuit missions and the wider Catholic Reformation, and became the root of Christianity's spread as a truly global religion in the centuries that followed.
prose_changes.new: Grew out of Catholic missions. The Portuguese came to Kongo in 1491 and the Franciscans to Mexico in 1524. The Jesuits went to Japan and China. Together they became one root of the spread of Christianity across the world in the centuries that followed.
prose_changes.reason: The old summary made every community grow from the Jesuits and the Catholic Reformation; Kongo (1491) and New Spain (Franciscans, 1524) began before both. Christianity was already in Asia and Africa, so 'the root' becomes 'one root'.

prose_changes.old: Grew from the Portuguese mission of 1491 and the Jesuit missions of the Catholic Reformation; the later prophetic movement of Dona Beatriz (1704) is its own entry.
prose_changes.new: Grew from the Portuguese mission of 1491. In 1547 Portugal sent Jesuits to help its bishop. The prophetic movement of Dona Beatriz, from 1704, later grew out of it.
prose_changes.reason: Jesuits arrived in a church that already had a bishop (1547 letter), so 'grew from the Jesuit missions' is wrong. 'is its own entry' was build narration.

prose_changes.old: Grew from Matteo Ricci's entry in 1583 and the Jesuit China mission; the rites controversy that followed belongs to the Society of Jesus and to later entries.
prose_changes.new: Grew from Matteo Ricci's arrival in 1583 and the Jesuit mission to China.
prose_changes.reason: 'belongs to the Society of Jesus and to later entries' was build narration, and the Society's own text does not discuss the rites quarrel.

prose_changes.old: These are the beginnings of Christianity as a genuinely global religion, and several of them were never broken. The hidden Christians of Japan kept a transmitted faith for roughly two hundred and fifty years without priests, and their villages are now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Latin American and Philippine Catholicism, with their processions, confraternities and local devotions, grew directly out of this period, and Kongolese Christianity shaped religion on both sides of the Atlantic, including among enslaved Africans in the Americas.
prose_changes.new: These are among the first steps of Christianity as a faith of the whole world, and several of them were never broken. The hidden Christians of Japan kept a faith handed down for about two hundred and fifty years with no priests. Their villages are now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Latin American and Philippine Catholicism grew straight out of this time, with their processions, brotherhoods and local saints. Kongo's Christians may also have shaped the beliefs of enslaved Africans in the Americas. But the writings of this time do not show it.
prose_changes.reason: The Atlantic claim has no source in the library or the movement's cited works (Thornton and Heywood are cited only on Kongo itself), so it becomes 'may have'. 'The beginnings' becomes 'among the first steps': the Church of the East had reached China in the 600s. Sentences split for reading level.

prose_changes.old: Grew directly out of Spanish colonial Catholicism, brought by friars following the start of Spanish rule in 1565.
prose_changes.new: Grew out of Spanish colonial Catholicism. Augustinian friars brought it from New Spain in 1565, and other orders came after them.
prose_changes.reason: Names where the friars came from, which the new New Spain link documents (Morga); 'directly' dropped, since several orders took part.

escalations: The mission-born movement is a label over four regional movements ('A label, not one movement - assessed per region'). This draft draws no links on the label itself: each relationship it names is carried on the regional movement, and its summary is rewritten region by region. Whether a label movement should also carry its own links (and so appear joined in the tree) is a method question no ruling covers; the only other label is progressive-christianity (era 10).
